overview: Cofán people live across the river and forest country of northeastern Ecuador and southern Colombia, where Amazonian lowlands approach the Andes. Their language is A’ingae. Hunting, fishing, forest knowledge and community leadership remain important, alongside changing forms of education, income and territorial protection.

periods.title: Oil development and territorial pressure
periods.summary: Oil exploration, roads and settlement disrupted Cofán territory around Dureno from the 1960s. Families marked boundaries and sought formal recognition of their land.

periods.title: Defending recognised lands
periods.summary: Dureno obtained land titles in 1978, but roads and further settlement continued to put pressure on its forest. Community protection developed alongside these changing conditions.

periods.title: Community management and continuing adaptation
periods.summary: Cofán land-management arrangements expanded in 2002 through the Bermejo reserve and cooperation in Cayambe-Coca. These agreements were stages in a continuing struggle to care for territory and sustain community life.

items.text: A study published in 2010 documented necklaces, baskets, cordage, dyes and other crafts during visits to Sábalo from 2007 to 2009. Makers combined plant materials with animal-derived elements and some plastic beads. Forest knowledge supported both household work and the sale of crafts.

The same study identified seeds, leaves, fruits and fibres among the materials used in craftwork. Necklaces drew on especially varied forest resources. Producing them required recognizing suitable materials and turning them into objects with uses beyond the plant itself.

In the early 2000s, coastal Ecuadorian boat makers taught Cofán builders to make fibreglass canoes. The project adapted an established form of river transport while reducing the need to cut large canoe trees. Some trainees developed boat-building businesses.

A later canoe project experimented with batteries, charging stations and electric motors. Its aim is to reduce dependence on fossil fuel and provide quieter river travel. The published account describes work in use and development, with wider commercial expansion still a goal.

sections.title: Research and recovery on the rivers

items.text: A turtle-recovery effort began in 1990 around the Aguarico and Zábalo rivers. Community members protected young turtles in pools before release, alongside restrictions on adult hunting and changes in egg collection. Recovery involved changing harvest practices as well as raising hatchlings.

Cofán researchers tested interviews, canoe-based turtle counts and surveys of nests on beaches. Comparing these methods made community observations available as a research record. The 2005 paper reported positive trends from two methods, without treating all observations as equally reliable measures.

A later study examined nesting records from 1994 to 2019. It found improving indicators for Podocnemis unifilis, but called for more work on age-specific population trends and the rarer P. expansa. Success with one species did not establish equal recovery for both.

Early boundary patrols relied on families giving time away from food production and paid work. The later Park Guard programme paid people to monitor territory and maintain access points. Supporting the guards’ households was part of making territorial protection sustainable.

Patrol groups brought people from different villages together, including older members who shared stories in forest camps. The programme’s account describes this as a setting for passing on historical and ecological knowledge while doing practical work.

Dureno’s conservation efforts included community hunting and fishing rules and an area where hunting was excluded so wildlife could reproduce. Food security and forest protection were connected concerns in the Field Museum’s 2007 account.

In Colombia, a participatory project worked with older Cofán women, healers, learners and families to document botanical knowledge. Interviews, visits to gardens and reserves, and plant illustrations contributed to a 2011 publication intended to help knowledge pass between generations.

Cofán tourism programmes train guides to explain forest life, manage journeys and communicate with visitors. The Survival Fund describes this as teaching outsiders through ecological expertise. Guiding combines inherited knowledge with language learning and the practical work of hosting people.

ending.text: Cofán communities continue in Ecuador and Colombia. Oil development, settlement and forest damage have restricted access to ancestral lands and resources. Community institutions, territorial protection and knowledge-sharing are responses to these pressures; they are part of a continuing history, not evidence of a people’s disappearance.
